title: Attosecond Transient Polarimetry
summary: We introduce elliptical-dichroic attosecond transient absorption spectroscopy (eDATAS), an ultrafast attosecond spectroscopy technique in which an atomic gas is probed by elliptically polarized attosecond and near-infrared pulses with an arbitrary angle between the polarization ellipses and a varying time-delay. Using perturbation theory, we show that the transient absorption signal factorizes into form factors whose dependence on pulse ellipticities and polarization-ellipse orientations are governed entirely by dipole selection rules: ellipticity sets the amplitudes of the interfering multiphoton pathways, while the relative orientations of the ellipses control the phase. We reinterpret circular- and linear-dichroic attosecond transient absorption spectroscopy as limiting cases of eDATAS, and validate the theory through an eDATAS measurement in helium, finding excellent agreement. Finally, we demonstrate that eDATAS can also serve as an in situ measurement of the polarization state of the XUV field, avoiding the need for a dedicated XUV polarimeter.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces elliptical-dichroic attosecond transient absorption spectroscopy (eDATAS), an ultrafast technique probing atomic gases with elliptically polarized attosecond and near-infrared pulses at arbitrary polarization-ellipse angles and time delays. Using perturbation theory, the authors show the transient absorption signal factorizes into form factors where pulse ellipticities set amplitudes of interfering multiphoton pathways and relative ellipse orientations control phase. Circular and linear dichroic versions are shown to be limiting cases, the theory is validated in helium with excellent agreement, and eDATAS doubles as an in situ XUV polarization-state measurement tool.
AI.motivation: To extend attosecond transient absorption spectroscopy beyond linear and circular dichroism to arbitrary elliptical polarization configurations, providing a general framework that connects polarization degrees of freedom (ellipticity and ellipse orientation) to dipole selection rules, and to enable in situ characterization of XUV polarization without a dedicated polarimeter.
AI.method: The technique employs elliptically polarized attosecond and near-infrared pulses with arbitrary angle between their polarization ellipses and tunable time delay. A perturbation theory analysis shows the transient absorption signal factorizes into form factors governed by dipole selection rules, with ellipticity controlling multiphoton pathway amplitudes and relative ellipse orientation controlling phase. The theory is validated by an eDATAS measurement in helium.
AI.result: The signal factorization was theoretically established and confirmed experimentally in helium with excellent agreement. eDATAS demonstrated capability to measure the polarization state of the XUV field in situ, eliminating the need for a dedicated XUV polarimeter. Circular- and linear-dichroic variants were recovered as limiting cases of the general framework.
AI.conclusion: eDATAS provides a unified, general framework for polarization-controlled attosecond transient absorption spectroscopy, with the polarization-ellipse geometry directly mapping onto selection-rule-governed pathway amplitudes and phases. The technique also offers a practical route for in situ XUV polarization metrology.

title: Magic Velocity Selection in Atom Interferometry
summary: Velocity-selective Raman transitions are widely used in atom interferometers to prepare atomic ensembles with narrowly defined momentum distributions. However, differential light shifts between atomic energy levels generate velocity distributions that are correlated with the Raman beam intensity, and therefore with the position of the atoms within the laser beam. We show that these spatially inhomogeneous velocity distributions interact with detuning-dependent systematic effects in a Bragg diffraction-based simultaneous conjugate Ramsey-Bordé interferometer. These interactions can induce systematic phase shifts of order 10 milliradians in the interferometer phase. We further identify a "magic" detuning for velocity selection and show that operating at this detuning suppresses the systematic phase shift. Magic velocity selection eliminates systematic errors arising from correlations between atom velocity and position, facilitating high-resolution atom interferometry experiments targeting sub-part-per-billion accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies that velocity-selective Raman transitions in atom interferometers create spatially inhomogeneous velocity distributions due to differential light shifts, which interact with detuning-dependent systematic effects in a Bragg-based simultaneous conjugate Ramsey-Bordé interferometer, causing systematic phase shifts of order 10 mrad. The authors discover a "magic" detuning for velocity selection that suppresses these systematic errors, enabling sub-part-per-billion accuracy.
AI.motivation: Velocity-selective Raman transitions prepare atomic ensembles with narrow momentum distributions, but differential light shifts create velocity-position correlations that can induce systematic phase errors in precision atom interferometry. Understanding and eliminating these errors is critical for high-accuracy measurements targeting sub-ppb precision.
AI.method: The authors analyze how spatially inhomogeneous velocity distributions (arising from Raman beam intensity gradients) couple to detuning-dependent systematic effects in a Bragg diffraction-based simultaneous conjugate Ramsey-Bordé interferometer. They derive the resulting systematic phase shifts and identify a "magic" detuning at which the velocity-selection systematic is suppressed.
AI.result: The interactions between spatially inhomogeneous velocity distributions and detuning-dependent systematic effects induce systematic phase shifts on the order of 10 milliradians. Operating at the identified "magic" detuning for velocity selection suppresses these systematic phase shifts.
AI.conclusion: Magic velocity selection eliminates systematic errors originating from correlations between atom velocity and position, enabling high-resolution atom interferometry experiments targeting sub-part-per-billion accuracy.

title: Note on proliferation transitions of non-Abelian anyons
summary: We study phase transitions out of a (2+1)d topological phase driven by the proliferation of anyons in a braided fusion subcategory. We describe a general theoretical framework for such transitions, in which the topological quantum field theory (TQFT) is coupled to dynamical matter associated with anyons in the subcategory. We interpret this construction using symmetry topological field theory (SymTFT), where the dynamics is localized on the symmetry boundary of the (3+1)d slab. We analyze several examples, and present explicit Chern-Simons-Higgs (CSH) field theories realizing the proliferation transitions. We also examine proliferation transitions that implement gauging of non-invertible one-form symmetry in the parent TQFT. This includes a general construction for ${\rm Rep}(G)$ one-form symmetry for a finite group $G$, and a CSH realization of the non-invertible one-form gauging ${\rm SU}(2)_{10}\rightarrow {\rm Spin}(5)_1$. We discuss which anyons proliferate at these transitions.

AI.tldr: This paper studies phase transitions out of (2+1)d topological phases driven by anyon proliferation in a braided fusion subcategory. The authors develop a general theoretical framework where the TQFT is coupled to dynamical anyonic matter, interpreted via SymTFT with dynamics localized on the symmetry boundary of a (3+1)d slab. They provide explicit Chern-Simons-Higgs (CSH) field theories realizing these transitions, including gauging of non-invertible one-form symmetry such as Rep(G) for finite groups and a specific SU(2)_10 → Spin(5)_1 transition.
AI.motivation: To develop a unified theoretical framework for understanding phase transitions out of topological phases induced by anyon proliferation, and to provide explicit field-theoretic constructions (Chern-Simons-Higgs theories) that realize such transitions, including the case of gauging non-invertible one-form symmetries.
AI.method: The authors couple the parent TQFT to dynamical matter fields associated with anyons in a braided fusion subcategory, and reinterpret this via SymTFT where the dynamics is localized on the symmetry boundary of a (3+1)d slab. They construct explicit Chern-Simons-Higgs theories for the proliferation transitions and analyze several examples, including a general construction for Rep(G) one-form symmetry and the non-invertible one-form gauging SU(2)_10 → Spin(5)_1.
AI.result: Explicit CSH field theories realizing anyon-proliferation transitions were constructed, including gauging of non-invertible Rep(G) one-form symmetry and the specific transition SU(2)_10 → Spin(5)_1. The paper identifies which anyons proliferate at these transitions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SymTFT-based framework provides a general and systematic description of anyon-proliferation phase transitions out of (2+1)d topological phases, with explicit CSH realizations covering both invertible and non-invertible symmetry gauging scenarios.

title: Quantum critical behavior in chains of hindered dipolar planar rotors
summary: We study the ground-state properties of linear chains of dipolar planar rotors hindered by a six-fold on-site potential, a model motivated by water molecules confined in the hexagonal cavities of beryl. Using density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations, we locate the quantum phase transition between the disordered and ferroelectrically ordered phases using the von Neumann entanglement entropy and the Binder ratio of the polarization. A sweep of the six-fold pinning strength shows that increasing hindrance shifts the critical dipolar coupling gc to smaller values. These results suggest that crystal-field hindrance can promote, rather than suppress, dipolar ordering. This work has implications for ferroelectricity and quantum-device tuning in confined molecular rotors

AI.tldr: A DMRG-based study of linear chains of dipolar planar rotors with a six-fold on-site potential (modeling water in beryl cavities) reveals a quantum phase transition between disordered and ferroelectric phases. Increasing the crystal-field hindrance shifts the critical dipolar coupling to smaller values, showing that hindrance promotes rather than suppresses dipolar ordering, with implications for ferroelectricity and quantum-device applications.
AI.motivation: To understand how crystal-field hindrance affects dipolar ordering in confined molecular rotors, motivated by water molecules in beryl's hexagonal cavities—challenging the intuitive assumption that stronger pinning suppresses ordering.
AI.method: Density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations on linear chains of dipolar planar rotors with a six-fold on-site potential, using the von Neumann entanglement entropy and the Binder ratio of polarization to locate the quantum phase transition and sweep the pinning strength.
AI.result: The critical dipolar coupling gc decreases monotonically as the six-fold pinning strength increases, indicating that crystal-field hindrance facilitates the onset of ferroelectric order.
AI.conclusion: Hindering potential from the crystal environment can promote, rather than suppress, dipolar ordering in confined molecular rotor chains, with practical implications for ferroelectric materials and tuning of quantum devices.

title: An LLM agent for end-to-end computational materials discovery
summary: The coordination of multi-scale tasks is an effective strategy for computational materials discovery, yet the repeated application of diverse algorithms and tools renders it challenging. We report MAESTRO, a large language model (LLM) agent system capable of executing the entire screening pipeline for metal-organic frameworks (MOFs). It processes a large body of MOF literature, links relevant publications to their crystal structures, and curates the results into a computation-ready database, which is then screened through a strategy of progressively increasing computational cost. The promising candidates identified for separation under wet flue gas conditions all originate from unrelated studies. By connecting the heterogeneous stages of computational materials discovery, the LLM-based agents of MAESTRO can operate across application domains and uncover high-performance materials that conventional screening approaches would be unlikely to consider.

AI.tldr: MAESTRO is an LLM agent system that automates the full computational screening pipeline for metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), from literature mining and structure linking to database curation and multi-scale screening, successfully identifying high-performance materials for separation under wet flue gas conditions.
AI.motivation: Multi-scale tasks are effective for computational materials discovery, but repeatedly applying diverse algorithms and tools across heterogeneous stages is challenging and limits the integration of different discovery steps.
AI.method: MAESTRO uses LLM-based agents to process MOF literature, link publications to crystal structures, curate results into a computation-ready database, and screen candidates through a strategy of progressively increasing computational cost.
AI.result: Promising candidates identified for separation under wet flue gas conditions all originate from unrelated studies, demonstrating the system's ability to uncover materials that conventional screening approaches would unlikely consider.
AI.conclusion: By connecting heterogeneous stages of computational materials discovery through LLM-based agents, MAESTRO can operate across application domains and discover high-performance materials beyond the reach of traditional screening workflows.

title: Criticality in Neural Network Function Space through Wilsonian Fixed Points and Finite-Width Corrections
comment: 30 pages, 16 figures, presented at the 3rd International Conference Mathematical Analysis and Applications in Science and Engineering (ICMASC) 2026 Conference, Portugal
summary: Neural networks can be studied not only as parameterized computational models but also as probability distributions over functions. In this paper we develop a Wilsonian interpretation of criticality in the neural network-quantum field theory correspondence, treating the infinite width Gaussian-process limit as a free field fixed point and finite width corrections as perturbations that create non-Gaussian interactions. In this way, we do not see the departure from infinite width as a small approximation error but as the process by which interaction, complexity, expressivity and phase-like behaviour enter neural network function space. Width, depth, activation nonlinearity, initialization variance, and training dynamics are considered as control parameters that change the effective action of the network ensemble. The critical regime is when the higher-order connected correlation functions become non-negligible, and when the finite width operators become relevant or marginal scaling factors, and when the function distribution becomes sensitive to scale-dependent structure. There we can view overparameterization as suppressing a relationship of interacting terms and we find that the critical structure of finite neural networks is given by finite-width effects. This framework is a theoretical basis for studying trainability, generalization, and architectural universality of neural network functions through Wilsonian fixed points, perturbations, and critical surfaces.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a Wilsonian renormalization-group interpretation of neural networks, treating the infinite-width Gaussian process limit as a free-field fixed point and finite-width corrections as perturbations generating non-Gaussian interactions. This reframes finite-width effects as the source of complexity, expressivity, and criticality in neural network function space.
AI.motivation: To provide a theoretical framework for understanding finite-width neural networks not as small approximations to the infinite-width Gaussian process limit, but as systems where finite-width corrections introduce genuine interactions, complexity, and phase-like behavior. The authors aim to establish a principled basis for studying trainability, generalization, and architectural universality.
AI.method: The paper applies Wilsonian renormalization-group concepts (fixed points, perturbations, critical surfaces, and scaling operators) to the neural network-quantum field theory correspondence. The infinite-width Gaussian process limit is identified as a free-field fixed point; finite-width corrections act as perturbative interactions. Width, depth, activation nonlinearity, initialization variance, and training dynamics serve as control parameters modifying the effective action. Criticality is defined by non-negligible higher-order connected correlation functions and relevant/marginal scaling of finite-width operators.
AI.result: The framework shows that the critical regime emerges when finite-width operators become relevant or marginal, higher-order correlations become significant, and the function distribution gains scale-dependent sensitivity. Overparameterization is interpreted as suppression of interacting terms, and the critical structure of finite networks is governed by finite-width effects.
AI.conclusion: The Wilsonian interpretation provides a theoretical basis for understanding trainability, generalization, and architectural universality of neural networks through renormalization-group fixed points, perturbations, and critical surfaces, unifying these phenomena within a field-theoretic framework.

title: Resolving positive semi-definiteness in physics-informed kernels for scientific machine learning
summary: Many modern machine learning models can be understood as kernel-based function-space models, including Gaussian processes and neural tangent kernels. In scientific machine learning, differential operators are increasingly used to encode physical structure directly into such models. However, it has remained unclear under which conditions these constructions are valid machine learning models, i.e. preserve positive semi-definiteness, and whether observed instabilities arise from ill-posed modeling or numerical effects. Here, we establish a simple and sufficient condition for positive semi-definiteness: for linear differential operators of order m, the base kernel must be m-times continuously differentiable. Crucially, this guarantee holds for operators with non-constant and even discontinuous coefficients. Examples are ubiquitous in physical systems, including diffusion, material elasticity, wave propagation in inhomogeneous media, and quantum systems. We conclude that remaining instabilities are attributable to numerical issues, providing a unifying validity foundation for operator-informed kernel methods.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a simple sufficient condition for the validity of operator-informed kernel methods: for linear differential operators of order m, the base kernel must be m-times continuously differentiable to preserve positive semi-definiteness. This guarantee holds even for operators with non-constant or discontinuous coefficients, and the authors conclude that remaining instabilities are numerical in origin rather than due to ill-posed modeling.
AI.motivation: While differential operators are increasingly used to encode physical structure into kernel-based models (e.g., Gaussian processes and neural tangent kernels) for scientific machine learning, it was unclear under what conditions these constructions remain valid machine learning models—specifically, when they preserve positive semi-definiteness—and whether observed instabilities stem from ill-posed modeling or numerical effects.
AI.method: The authors derive and prove a simple sufficient condition for positive semi-definiteness: for a linear differential operator of order m, the base kernel must be m-times continuously differentiable. The proof covers operators with non-constant and even discontinuous coefficients, which are pervasive in physical systems such as diffusion, elasticity, wave propagation in inhomogeneous media, and quantum systems.
AI.result: The paper establishes the sufficiency condition guaranteeing positive semi-definiteness of operator-kernel compositions, valid for a broad class of linear differential operators including those with non-constant and discontinuous coefficients. Consequently, it is shown that remaining observed instabilities are attributable to numerical issues rather than to ill-posed modeling.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a unifying validity foundation for operator-informed kernel methods, clarifying that the theoretical validity is guaranteed under smoothness conditions on the base kernel, and that practical instabilities should be addressed as numerical challenges.

title: Two-dimensional percolation with algebraically decaying interactions II: Critical exponents in the long-range regime
summary: We present a comprehensive Monte Carlo study of two-dimensional bond percolation with algebraically decaying connection probabilities $p(r)\propto 1/r^{2+σ}$, establishing the universality diagram in the long-range (LR) regime for $σ\le2$. Using the event-based ensemble method, we simulate systems with linear sizes up to $L=16384$ and investigate three universality regimes: LR Wilson--Fisher (WF) A ($1<σ\le2$), LR Wilson--Fisher B ($2/3<σ\le1$), and LR mean-field (MF) ($0<σ\le2/3$). In the LR-WF-B regime, the anomalous dimension is consistent with $η=2-σ$, in agreement with mathematical results for $2/3<σ<1$, while the correlation-length exponent $ν(σ)$ exhibits nontrivial, non-Gaussian variation. In the LR-WF-A regime, although $η$ remains close to $2-σ$ for smaller $σ$, statistically resolvable deviations $δη(σ)=η-(2-σ)>0$ start to appear near $σ\simeq3/2$ and grow toward the short-range crossover at $σ=2$. Finally, by complementing the event-based simulations with conventional ensemble simulations, we reveal the coexistence of complete-graph asymptotics and LR Gaussian-fixed-point scaling in the LR-MF regime. These results further clarify the critical properties in long-range percolation and provide crucial benchmarks for long-range statistical systems.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive Monte Carlo study of two-dimensional long-range bond percolation with algebraically decaying probabilities, mapping the universality diagram across three regimes (LR-WF-A, LR-WF-B, LR-MF) using systems up to L=16384.
AI.motivation: To establish the complete universality diagram for long-range percolation in the σ≤2 regime, clarifying critical properties, anomalous dimensions, and correlation-length exponents that have remained incompletely characterized across different long-range regimes.
AI.method: Event-based ensemble Monte Carlo simulations of 2D bond percolation with p(r)∝1/r^{2+σ}, with system sizes up to L=16384, complemented by conventional ensemble simulations; analysis across three universality regimes (LR-WF-A for 1<σ≤2, LR-WF-B for 2/3<σ≤1, LR-MF for 0<σ≤2/3).
AI.result: In LR-WF-B, η=2-σ confirms mathematical predictions, while ν(σ) shows nontrivial non-Gaussian variation. In LR-WF-A, η≈2-σ for smaller σ but statistically resolvable positive deviations δη(σ)>0 emerge near σ≈3/2 and grow toward the short-range crossover at σ=2. In LR-MF, coexistence of complete-graph asymptotics and LR Gaussian-fixed-point scaling is revealed.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a complete and precise universality diagram for long-range percolation, revealing deviations from the expected η=2-σ in the LR-WF-A regime and novel coexistence phenomena in the LR-MF regime, offering crucial benchmarks for long-range statistical systems.

title: Real-time ESR tracking for sub-micron 3D magnetic mapping with VB- quantum sensors in hexagonal boron nitride
summary: The discovery of spin-dependent luminescent properties of negatively charged boron-vacancy centers ($V^-_B$) in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) enabled a new platform for quantum sensing with van der Waals materials. Particularly, the possibility of performing optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) for determining the electron spin resonance (ESR) frequencies of hBN color centers became a strong tool for quantum sensing of magnetic fields with submicrometric resolution. However, due to low ODMR contrast, current techniques proposed for mapping DC magnetic fields require hours of integration to obtain a magnetic image of a micron-sized region. In this work, we report the implementation of a frequency-tracking approach for real-time monitoring of ESR frequencies of localized $V^-_B$ centers in hBN. With this technique, magnetic field monitoring was used to map the field pattern generated by a micron-sized conical magnetic tip in only a few minutes. By controlling the magnetic sample's position relative to the quantum sensor, three-dimensional magnetic mapping of the field was achieved with diffraction-limited resolution and shot-noise-limited sensitivity of 54 $μ$T$/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$. Magnetic field gradients of 3.6 $\pm$ 0.2 $μ$T/nm were measured with our system, in which a maximum detected field rate of 6 mT/s was achieved. The results of this study establish spin resonance frequency-tracking as a viable technique and fast method for minute-scale magnetic imaging, reducing acquisition times by at least one order of magnitude if compared to conventional techniques.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a frequency-tracking approach for real-time monitoring of electron spin resonance (ESR) frequencies of negatively charged boron-vacancy (V_B^-) centers in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), enabling fast magnetic field mapping with diffraction-limited resolution and shot-noise-limited sensitivity of 54 μT/√Hz. This method reduces acquisition times by at least an order of magnitude compared to conventional ODMR-based techniques.
AI.motivation: Current ODMR-based techniques for mapping DC magnetic fields using V_B^- centers in hBN suffer from low ODMR contrast, requiring hours of integration to obtain a magnetic image of a micron-sized region. A faster method is needed for practical quantum sensing applications.
AI.method: The authors implement a frequency-tracking approach for real-time monitoring of ESR frequencies of localized V_B^- centers in hBN. The magnetic sample's position is controlled relative to the quantum sensor to achieve three-dimensional magnetic mapping. The system measures magnetic field gradients and achieves a maximum detected field rate of 6 mT/s.
AI.result: The frequency-tracking technique maps the field pattern generated by a micron-sized conical magnetic tip in only a few minutes. Three-dimensional magnetic mapping was achieved with diffraction-limited resolution and shot-noise-limited sensitivity of 54 μT/√Hz. Magnetic field gradients of 3.6 ± 0.2 μT/nm were measured, with a maximum detected field rate of 6 mT/s.
AI.conclusion: Spin resonance frequency-tracking is established as a viable and fast method for minute-scale magnetic imaging, reducing acquisition times by at least one order of magnitude compared to conventional techniques.

title: Non-reciprocal heat transfer advances flexible thermoelectric devices
summary: Complex heat dissipation assemblies, inferior performance, and limited flexibility are the primary constraints impeding the wide application and commercialization of conventional flexible thermoelectric devices in wearable electronics and other high-end cooling scenarios. In this work, we report a non-conventional design for flexible thermoelectric devices which can reduce the temperature to -7.03 at room temperature without external heat sink, achieving a cooling temperature drop of 29.25. The design is based on non-reciprocal heat transfer, integrated with thermally conductive composites and screen-printing technologies. This approach takes advantage of directional heat flow, thereby eliminating the need for complex heat sink networks, which extend the applications of flexible thermoelectric devices from personal thermal management to more broader fields such as home healthcare and emergency first aid.

AI.tldr: A non-conventional flexible thermoelectric device design based on non-reciprocal heat transfer achieves a cooling temperature drop of 29.25°C (reaching -7.03°C at room temperature) without external heat sinks, using thermally conductive composites and screen-printing technology, enabling broader applications in wearable electronics, healthcare, and emergency first aid.
AI.motivation: Conventional flexible thermoelectric devices are constrained by complex heat dissipation assemblies, inferior performance, and limited flexibility, which impede their commercialization in wearable electronics and high-end cooling applications.
AI.method: The design employs non-reciprocal heat transfer, integrated with thermally conductive composites and screen-printing technologies, to achieve directional heat flow that eliminates the need for complex heat sink networks.
AI.result: The device reduces temperature to -7.03°C at room temperature without an external heat sink, achieving a cooling temperature drop of 29.25°C.
AI.conclusion: This approach extends the applications of flexible thermoelectric devices beyond personal thermal management to broader fields such as home healthcare and emergency first aid.

title: Perspectives on Magnetic/Superconductor Hybrid Systems: Long-range Electromagnetic Phenomena Induced by Proximity Effect and Interfacial Spin-orbit Coupling
comment: Published in Journal of Applied Physics, original version of the paper before copyediting, 21 pages, 16 figures
summary: In this Perspective we review recent achievements in physics and applications of hybrid superconductor-ferromagnet structures. In particular, we focus on the manifestations of the electromagnetic phenomena in these systems originating from the response of the induced superconducting correlations modified by the exchange field and additional effects coming from the interface Rashba-type spin-orbit coupling. The review includes the long-range electromagnetic proximity effect and related modification of magnetic textures, spontaneous currents, properties of vortex matter and its interaction with magnetic ordering, spin-galvanic, photogalvanic and nonreciprocal transport phenomena in exemplary hybrid systems. We also present our views on the future development of this field including both the theoretical challenges and promising opportunities for fundamental experiments.

AI.tldr: A Perspective review of physics and applications in hybrid superconductor-ferromagnet structures, focusing on electromagnetic phenomena arising from induced superconducting correlations modified by exchange fields and Rashba spin-orbit coupling, covering long-range proximity effects, magnetic textures, vortex matter, and spin-galvanic/nonreciprocal transport, plus future outlook.
AI.motivation: To consolidate and review recent achievements in hybrid superconductor-ferromagnet structures, emphasizing the electromagnetic phenomena that emerge from the interplay of induced superconducting correlations with exchange fields and Rashba-type spin-orbit coupling, and to outline future theoretical and experimental directions.
AI.method: A Perspective-style review synthesizing recent work on hybrid superconductor-ferromagnet systems, organized around electromagnetic phenomena such as the long-range proximity effect, magnetic texture modification, spontaneous currents, vortex matter physics, and spin-galvanic, photogalvanic, and nonreciprocal transport effects.
AI.result: The review presents a comprehensive survey of electromagnetic effects in superconductor-ferromagnet hybrids, including long-range electromagnetic proximity effects, modified magnetic textures, spontaneous currents, vortex-magnetic ordering interactions, and various galvanic and nonreciprocal transport phenomena across exemplary systems.
AI.conclusion: The authors provide perspectives on future development, highlighting theoretical challenges and promising opportunities for fundamental experiments in this field.

title: Distinguishing Mott and strain-induced anisotropic semimetals in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene using Landau level spectroscopy
summary: Recent quantum twisting microscopy experiments [1] have provided unprecedented momentum- and energy-resolved imaging of magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, revealing a stark dichotomy between the heavy and light electronic characters of its narrow bands. In this work, we provide a sharp distinguishing criterion between the two most likely candidate states that exhibit spectroscopic features consistent with the experimental results. Focusing on charge neutrality, these states are 1) the 'Mott semimetal', governed by strong dynamical correlations, and 2) the 'strain-induced anisotropic semimetal', characterized by weak Hartree-Fock effects. We demonstrate that an out-of- plane magnetic field serves as a sharp discriminating probe based on the expected Landau level gap size hierarchy. We find that the strain-induced anisotropic semimetal has a robust gap hierarchy where the Chern C gaps, Δ_C , decrease in order Δ_{\pm 4} > Δ_{\pm 8} > Δ_{\pm 12}. In contrast, for the Mott semimetal, Δ_{\pm 4} remains the largest gap, while the relative magnitude of the C = \pm 8, \pm 12 gaps depends sensitively on the applied magnetic field. We test the robustness of these results against strain orientation and lattice relaxation finding consistency between the gap hierarchy of the strained semimetal and previous incompressibility measurements at finite magnetic field [2].

AI.tldr: The paper provides a sharp distinguishing criterion between two candidate states of magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene at charge neutrality: the 'Mott semimetal' (strong dynamical correlations) and the 'strain-induced anisotropic semimetal' (weak Hartree-Fock effects). Using out-of-plane magnetic field as a discriminating probe, they show the strain-induced semimetal exhibits a robust Landau level gap hierarchy Δ_{±4} > Δ_{±8} > Δ_{±12}, while the Mott semimetal shows sensitive field-dependence of higher Chern gaps. Results are consistent with prior incompressibility measurements at finite magnetic field.
AI.motivation: Quantum twisting microscopy experiments have revealed a stark dichotomy between heavy and light electronic characters in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene's narrow bands. The authors aim to distinguish between the two most likely candidate states consistent with these spectroscopic features: the Mott semimetal and the strain-induced anisotropic semimetal.
AI.method: The authors use an out-of-plane magnetic field as a discriminating probe and analyze the expected Landau level gap size hierarchy (Chern C gaps, Δ_C) for both candidate states. They compute gap hierarchies for the strain-induced anisotropic semimetal and the Mott semimetal, testing robustness against strain orientation and lattice relaxation.
AI.result: The strain-induced anisotropic semimetal exhibits a robust gap hierarchy Δ_{±4} > Δ_{±8} > Δ_{±12}. For the Mott semimetal, Δ_{±4} remains the largest gap, but the relative magnitude of C = ±8, ±12 gaps depends sensitively on the applied magnetic field. The strain-induced semimetal's hierarchy is consistent with previous incompressibility measurements at finite magnetic field.
AI.conclusion: The Landau level gap hierarchy under an out-of-plane magnetic field serves as a sharp experimental discriminator between the Mott semimetal and strain-induced anisotropic semimetal states, with the strained semimetal hierarchy showing consistency with previous finite-field measurements.

title: $\mathcal{PT}$ and anti-$\mathcal{PT}$ phase transitions in a trimerized Su--Schrieffer--Heeger chain with nonreciprocal Rashba spin-orbit coupling
summary: We theoretically investigate a one-dimensional trimerized Su--Schrieffer--Heeger chain with three sublattices per unit cell subjected to a nonreciprocal Rashba spin-orbit coupling. Invoking a spin-flip symmetry, the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian decomposes into two independent spin sectors, enabling a spin-resolved analysis of non-Hermitian skin effects and system symmetries. We identify a rich phase diagram consisting of four bulk phases and two edge-state phases. The bulk phases include fully $\mathcal{PT}$-unbroken (real-spectrum) and fully anti-$\mathcal{PT}$-unbroken (imaginary-spectrum) regimes, as well as two mixed phases where one band remains on the real or imaginary axis while the other two form complex-conjugate pairs. The two edge-state phases correspond to topological edge modes with either $\mathcal{PT}$-unbroken (real) or anti-$\mathcal{PT}$-unbroken (imaginary) energies. Using non-Bloch band theory and Cardano's method, we derive closed-form expressions for phase boundaries and establish the bulk-edge correspondence for each spin sector. Calculations of Berry phase and directional inverse participation ratios confirm our analytical predictions. Our results provide a minimal platform for realizing spin-resolved non-Hermitian topology and edge-selective symmetry preservation, in which the bulk and edge states belong to distinct symmetry classes.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically studies a one-dimensional trimerized Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain with nonreciprocal Rashba spin-orbit coupling, where a spin-flip symmetry decomposes the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian into independent spin sectors. Using non-Bloch band theory and Cardano's method, the authors map out a phase diagram with four bulk phases (PT-unbroken, anti-PT-unbroken, and two mixed phases) and two edge-state phases, establishing bulk-edge correspondence and confirming predictions via Berry phase and inverse participation ratio calculations.
AI.motivation: To provide a minimal theoretical platform for realizing spin-resolved non-Hermitian topology and edge-selective symmetry preservation, where bulk and edge states belong to distinct symmetry classes.
AI.method: The authors invoke a spin-flip symmetry to decouple the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian into two spin sectors, enabling spin-resolved analysis. They employ non-Bloch band theory and Cardano's method to derive closed-form phase boundaries, and use Berry phase and directional inverse participation ratios to confirm analytical predictions.
AI.result: A rich phase diagram with four bulk phases (fully PT-unbroken, fully anti-PT-unbroken, and two mixed phases) and two edge-state phases (topological edge modes with real or imaginary energies) is identified, with bulk-edge correspondence established for each spin sector.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a minimal platform for spin-resolved non-Hermitian topology, demonstrating that bulk and edge states can preserve different symmetry classes, with the predictions confirmed by numerical calculations.

title: Carrier Capture at Defects from Finite-Temperature Lattice Dynamics
summary: Defect-assisted carrier capture is commonly described within nonradiative multiphonon (NMP) theory using normal modes of the equilibrium defect structure. This description becomes inadequate when finite-temperature lattice fluctuations explore configurations that cannot be represented by a fixed normal-mode basis. Here, we present a trajectory-based method for calculating carrier capture rate from first principles, which allows lattice relaxation and electron--lattice coupling matrix element to be reconstructed directly from correlation functions of finite-temperature lattice dynamics. For hole capture at C$_\mathrm{N}$ in GaN within harmonic regime, the method reproduces static NMP results including mode mixing and agrees with experiment. title: Graphon Spin Systems as Exactly Solvable Models
summary:
Graphons are measurable functions used to describe the asymptotic behavior of convergent graph families. Originally motivated by problems in combinatorics and graph theory, graphons have found numerous applications in the modeling and analysis of dynamical processes on networks.
  In this work, we use graphons to formulate the Ising model on convergent graph sequences, which include many network topologies common in applications. We derive the mean-field limit for the resulting model and obtain exact results for phase transitions in such systems. Specifically, we show that the critical temperatures of the Ising model on graphons are determined by the eigenvalues of the Hilbert-Schmidt operator associated with the graph limit. For many important network topologies, these eigenvalues can be computed explicitly.
  We illustrate our results with three representative random network models: Erdős-Rényi, small-world, and power-law. In the small-world case, we demonstrate phase transitions to both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic phases, as well as coexistence of local minima of the free energy. The latter gives rise to multistability, as confirmed by Monte Carlo simulations.
  The results of this work demonstrate that the Ising model on graphons combines the analytical tractability of exactly solvable mean-field models with the ability to accommodate a broad range of network topologies. We expect that the use of graphons in spin models will lead to new insights into the statistical physics of interacting systems on complex networks.

title: Symmetry Adapted Hierarchical Equations of Motion for Exact Simulations of Large Polariton Systems
summary: Hierarchical equations of motion(HEOM) provide exact dynamics of open quantum systems coupled to harmonic baths, but their computational cost becomes prohibitive for systems with many independent local environments. In this work, we develop a symmetry-adapted HEOM formalism to significantly reduce the computational cost for the permutationally invariant Holstein-Tavis-Cummings (HTC) model. The method removes redundant information in two stages. First, all auxiliary density operators (ADOs) related only by relabeling identical molecules and their bath channels are replaced by a single canonical occupation-pattern representative. Second, molecules with the same local hierarchy occupation produce repeated matrix elements within each representative, allowing only the distinct complex variables to be propagated instead of the full (N + 1) $\times$ (N + 1) ADO matrices. The resulting matrix-free equations are evaluated using precomputed connections and molecular multiplicities. At fixed hierarchy depth L and number of bath correlation exponentials m, the number of canonical representatives becomes independent of the ensemble size for N $\geq$ L and the number of unique variables saturates for N $\geq$ L + 2. The formulation easily extends to multiple-exponential bath decompositions, arbitrary initial density operators, static disorders, and cavity loss. Our benchmarks reproduce conventional HEOM dynamics while requiring far fewer propagated variables and substantially less memory.

This yields reduced computational cost and memory while reproducing exact conventional HEOM dynamics.

title: Quantum Wake Dynamics from Distinct Spectroscopic Perturbations
summary: Quantum wake dynamics in quantum magnets have recently been inferred from the dynamical spin structure factor, which probes only a restricted class of local perturbations. Here, we show that resonant inelastic x-ray scattering (RIXS) selection rules act as an operator filter on fractionalized excitations, producing distinct quantum wakes in the spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain. Using explicit real-time evolution of single-spin and spin-conserving bond correlators, we find that the conventional spin response propagates up to the maximum spinon velocity, $v_s=\fracπ{2} J$, whereas the bond channels concentrate their spectral weight into a slower dominant wake with $v\simeq 0.92 J$, while weaker components remain bounded by the full spinon light cone. The corresponding momentum- and frequency-resolved responses map onto experimentally accessible RIXS channels, demonstrating that different spectroscopic perturbations resolve complementary pathways of many-body propagation beyond the neutron-scattering spin structure factor. Their inelastic spectral weights further provide access to quantum Fisher information, while equal-time bond sum rules connect the same spectroscopic channels to the ground-state energy. Because the same correlators can be prepared and measured on quantum hardware, they also define direct, experimentally anchored benchmarks for quantum simulations, particularly in frustrated and higher-dimensional magnets where controlled classical real-time calculations become challenging.

title: Electrostatic Influence of Diamond Heat-Spreaders on GaN FET Performance
summary: Diamond, with its exceptional thermal conductivity, is widely explored as a heat spreader to improve thermal management in GaN-based power and RF electronics. In this work, we use Sentaurus TCAD to model AlGaN/GaN HEMTs with integrated diamond heat spreaders, incorporating advanced physical models such as thermal boundary resistance (TBR) and temperature-dependent bandgap narrowing. While diamond significantly enhances heat dissipation, our simulations reveal an important but often overlooked tradeoff: electrostatic modulation at the diamond and semiconductor interface. We initially modeled a p-GaN HEMT with all-around diamond integration and show agreement to the experimentally reported electrothermal benefits of diamond heat spreader integration. However, we observe strong band bending at the diamond/GaN interface alongside electric field generation and increased valence band energy in diamond. As a result, an interfacial hole accumulation region forms at the GaN surface, altering vertical transport and hindering current injection which prevents high on-state current. These results indicate that although diamond improves thermal performance, it can also actively influence the electrostatics of the transistor. To address both the elevated TBR and the undesired interfacial band bending, we propose the incorporation of an engineered interlayer. Building on our Sentaurus TCAD results, we develop a Silvaco TCAD TLM test structure to characterize the extent of the hole accumulation region formation and give insight to future studies on mitigation through interlayer development.

title: A non-local power-law baseline for transient flux penetration in YBCO films: parameter degeneracy and constitutive limitations
summary: We assess whether a non-local thin-film model with a bounded, constant-exponent power law can reproduce high-speed magneto-optical measurements of transient flux penetration in a $3\times3$~mm$^2$ YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{7-δ}$ film. The model is solved forward in physical units and used as a controlled constitutive baseline. The critical sheet current is constrained by the final penetration geometry, while the criterion field and creep exponent are constrained by the turnover and relaxation times. The calibration reveals an intrinsic degeneracy: the turnover time depends primarily on the product of the criterion field and saturation parameter, equivalently on the saturated sheet resistivity, so these quantities cannot be identified independently. After parameterizing this degeneracy, the model captures a guarded-current turnover near 22~ms, a relaxation constant of 41.2~ms compared with the measured 37.5 and 43.7~ms, and a late maximum approximately 0.92~mm from the film edge. The amplitude remains discrepant: the calculated transient maximum is $1.90J_{c0}$ and the peak-to-225-ms ratio is 2.13, compared with the reported 1.20. This excess persists under changes in the creep exponent, the degenerate parameter direction, the Kim field dependence, and mesh resolution. Matching the measured ratio through the criterion field would require a value about three orders of magnitude below the conventional scale, while spatial exclusion sufficient to match it would remove the edge peak itself. We also decompose the electric field into irrotational and solenoidal parts and quantify the boundary layer where spectral and finite-difference forms of Faraday's law disagree. The results establish a reproducible non-local power-law baseline and identify limitations of the bounded, constant-exponent constitutive family rather than of non-local thin-film electrodynamics.

title: Electronic Toroidal Metals: Landau Theory and Magnetoelectric Fingerprints
summary: Toroidal order is a higher-rank multipolar order whose intrinsic realization in itinerant-electron systems remains unexplored. Here, we develop a generic theory of the electronic toroidal metal (ETM), in which toroidal order emerges spontaneously from electronic degrees of freedom near the Fermi surfaces. Because candidate toroidal bilinears can overlap by symmetry with the uniform charge current, we formulate a projected instability criterion that removes the noncondensable current component. Within this current-orthogonal sector, we identify a soft collective mode in the $\mathcal{P}$-odd and $\mathcal{T}$-odd particle-hole channel and demonstrate that ETM arises as a Fermi-liquid instability. We then define the toroidal moment in an itinerant system through the antisymmetric magnetoelectric response tensor. We further establish an intimate connection between this response and the topology of pseudospin texture: the rearrangement of pseudospin vortices changes the winding structure of the Fermi surfaces and markedly enhances the magnetoelectric response. ETM also exhibits characteristic nonlinear charge transport, including a pronounced enhancement of its interband quantum-geometric contribution. Our results establish ETM as a distinct metallic Landau phase and provide a general framework for understanding toroidal order generated by itinerant electrons.

title: Interband plasmons due to Mexican hat dispersion in two-dimensional materials with inverted bands
summary: Two-dimensional topological materials with Mexican-hat dispersion exhibit numerous nontrivial features, such as double-valued isoenergetic contours in k-space, strong mixing of electron and hole states, a van Hove singularity in the density of states, and specific quantum geometric properties. We find that, due to these features, Mexican-hat dispersion significantly strengthens interband plasmons, reduces their damping, and gives rise to an additional branch of the plasmon spectrum when electron-hole symmetry is broken. The plasmon spectra are limited to a finite range of the wave vector, the boundaries of which depend on the strength of the electron-electron interaction. We also reveal a relationship between the features of the plasmon spectrum and singularities of the joint density of states with a finite plasmon wave vector q, as well as features of the interband quantum metric, which also depend on q.

title: Revealing the Role of Confined Molecular H$_2$ in the Passivation of Defective Silicon Using First-Principles Simulations
summary: The passivation of silicon dangling bonds by hydrogen is a crucial requirement for silicon-based optoelectronic technology, especially for solar cells. Recent experiments on intense light soaking of silicon heterojunction solar cells unveiled interesting dynamical aspects of hydrogen passivation that are linked to Si-H bond breaking and repassivation. These processes take place predominantly in porous regions near the amorphous/crystalline interface, where hydrogen can exist in molecular form. This work addresses the question of whether molecular H$_2$ directly participates in Si-H depassivation and repassivation. Using density functional theory, we calculate and compare formation energies of point defects, multivacancy cavities and the Si(100) surface to identify relevant passivated and depassivated states. Furthermore, we employ nudged elastic band calculations to determine the activation barriers of the corresponding pathways. We find that sufficient local free volume enables a direct double-H pathway for depassivation through the formation of confined molecular H$_2$. Despite involving the breaking of two Si-H bonds, the double-H process can be energetically and kinetically competitive with the single-H process and can exhibit a reverse repassivation barrier as low as $0.15\,$eV under p-type conditions. These findings provide a plausible atomistic explanation for passivation recovery during light soaking and illuminated annealing in porous regions near amorphous/crystalline silicon interfaces.

title: Conservation capacity of local learning rules in physical networks
summary: How many memories can a local learning rule protect, and what fixes the number? Physical learning rules train resistive networks through local measurements, and the standard rules conserve a mass-like function of the conductances, a law whose general form was posed as an open problem with the expectation that no useful solution theory exists. We answer it, in the direction the expectation ran against, and the answer is a capacity theory. The Tellegen identity behind the conserved mass localizes: the feedback state is pinned to zero at the inputs, so every sector of the circuit that the input electrodes separate carries its own private conserved mass, by an argument consuming only Kirchhoff's law and that boundary condition, hence valid for arbitrary nonlinear branch laws. The number of independent sector masses is a topological property of the circuit, bounded by the number of output electrodes. An untrainable element can destroy the mass of its own sector and of no other, which says where fixed nonlinear components may be placed; per-edge learning rates select which functionals are conserved and never how many; and adjoint coupled learning, which clamps its outputs before measuring, drains every output-carrying sector at a rate set by the squared output multipliers. In linear circuits we then classify the identities: exact rational computation over all 502 circuits on up to five vertices with two inputs and one or two outputs, and hundreds of larger ones, yields a closed-form count, proved on that family and conjectured in general, with the sector statement a theorem at every circuit size. The anticipated series-parallel polynomial laws appear as exactly the series-class cubic differences, and the number the opening question asks for is a budget: one designed mass per sector, the differences the topology donates, and one broadcast scalar for each protected functional beyond.

title: Scalable photoexcitation-induced molecular dynamics with machine-learned Hamiltonians
summary: Ultrafast photoexcitation offers a controllable route to steer structural dynamics in solids, yet predicting how nonequilibrium electronic excitation drives lattice motion across extended spatial and temporal scales remains a major computational challenge. Here we introduce time-dependent ab-initio propagation with electronic machine learning (TDAP-eML), a framework that explicitly incorporates electronic evolution into scalable simulations of photoexcitation-induced lattice dynamics. By integrating machine-learned electronic structure with atomistic propagation, TDAP-eML describes how photoexcitation reshapes the evolving energy landscapes and forces governing structural motion. Across representative examples including silicon and FeSe, the framework reproduces key photoexcited lattice responses obtained from first-principles time-dependent density functional theory calculations and captures coherent phonon dynamics together with their dependence on excitation conditions. Its computational advantage increases with system size, reaching nearly three orders of magnitude reduction in computational cost for the large systems examined. TDAP-eML thus establishes a scalable framework for coupled electronic and lattice evolution, linking nonequilibrium excitation to photoinduced forces, predictive structural dynamics, and experimentally accessible observables.

AI.tldr: Introduces TDAP-eML, a framework combining time-dependent ab-initio propagation with electronic machine learning to enable scalable simulations of photoexcitation-induced lattice dynamics in solids, achieving up to three orders of magnitude computational speedup while reproducing first-principles results.
AI.motivation: Predicting how nonequilibrium electronic excitation drives lattice motion across extended spatial and temporal scales remains a major computational challenge due to the high cost of first-principles time-dependent methods.
AI.method: Integrates machine-learned electronic structure with atomistic propagation to explicitly incorporate electronic evolution into scalable simulations of photoexcitation-induced lattice dynamics.
AI.result: Reproduces photoexcited lattice responses from time-dependent density functional theory in silicon and FeSe, captures coherent phonon dynamics and excitation-condition dependence, and achieves nearly three orders of magnitude computational cost reduction that scales favorably with system size.
AI.conclusion: TDAP-eML establishes a scalable framework for coupled electronic and lattice evolution, linking nonequilibrium excitation to photoinduced forces, predictive structural dynamics, and experimentally accessible observables.

title: Meandering stripes in the frustrated $J_1$-$J_2$ Ising model on the honeycomb lattice
summary: We study the frustrated $J_1$-$J_2$ Ising model on the honeycomb lattice with ferromagnetic nearest-neighbor couplings fixed at $J_1=1$ and strong antiferromagnetic next-nearest-neighbor interactions, i.e., $J_2 \leq -1/4$. Little is known for this range of $J_2$, whereas for less negative values of $J_2$ the system orders ferromagnetically at low temperatures and appears to remain in the Ising universality class. In previous work it was shown that the model has a largely degenerate ground state, and it was conjectured that there is some kind of phase transition. We introduce a complex-valued nematic order parameter, which can differentiate between the high-temperature paramagnetic phase and the observed partially-disordered stripe phase at lower temperatures. Configurations in this phase consist of stripes of spins parallel with respect to one lattice direction, which collectively meander along the remaining two, producing partially disordered ground states. The sharp peaks in the specific heat observed in earlier work only appear when using periodic boundary conditions and are absent for free boundaries. Additionally, we reveal a striking dependence of the behavior on the aspect ratio of the considered samples. Ultimately, even a careful finite-size scaling analysis for $J_2 = -0.5$ and $J_2 = -1$ is unable to clearly discern between a crossover without any singularities and some form of continuous transition, including the possibility of an infinite-order transition of the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) type. For $J_2=-1/4$ we find that the system remains disordered at all temperatures and that it exhibits a finite ground-state entropy per site, for which our simulations provide the accurate asymptotic estimate $S(T=0)/N = 0.230\,960\,93(14)$ in the thermodynamic limit $N\rightarrow\infty$.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the frustrated J1-J2 Ising model on the honeycomb lattice with ferromagnetic nearest-neighbor (J1=1) and strong antiferromagnetic next-nearest-neighbor couplings (J2 ≤ -1/4). Using a complex-valued nematic order parameter, the authors characterize a partially-disordered stripe phase and find that specific heat peaks depend on boundary conditions and aspect ratio. Finite-size scaling at J2=-0.5 and -1 cannot clearly distinguish between a crossover and a continuous (possibly BKT-type) transition, while at J2=-1/4 the system remains disordered at all temperatures with finite ground-state entropy per site estimated as 0.23096093(14).
AI.motivation: Little is known about the honeycomb-lattice J1-J2 Ising model in the strongly frustrated regime J2 ≤ -1/4, where a largely degenerate ground state was previously observed and a phase transition was conjectured but not characterized.
AI.method: The authors introduce a complex-valued nematic order parameter capable of distinguishing between the high-temperature paramagnetic phase and the low-temperature partially-disordered stripe phase. They perform simulations with both periodic and free boundary conditions, examine dependence on sample aspect ratio, and carry out careful finite-size scaling analysis for J2=-0.5 and J2=-1, plus entropy estimation at J2=-1/4.
AI.result: Sharp specific-heat peaks appear only with periodic boundary conditions and vanish for free boundaries, with a striking dependence on aspect ratio. Finite-size scaling at J2=-0.5 and -1 cannot conclusively distinguish between a crossover without singularities and some continuous transition, including possible infinite-order BKT-type transition. At J2=-1/4 the system is disordered at all temperatures with finite ground-state entropy per site, asymptotically estimated as S(T=0)/N=0.23096093(14).
AI.conclusion: The nature of the phase transition in the strongly frustrated regime remains ambiguous, possibly being a crossover or an unconventional continuous/BKT transition; at the critical frustration J2=-1/4 the system exhibits disorder at all temperatures with a precisely estimated finite ground-state entropy, reflecting the high degeneracy of the ground-state manifold.

title: Accurate and Transferable Intermolecular Potential Based on Machine-Learned Molecular Electron Density
summary: Machine-learned force fields (MLFFs) contain many learnable parameters and therefore require large training datasets. This poses a challenge for developing highly accurate, general-purpose MLFFs because generating high-quality ab initio reference data is computationally expensive. Classical empirical potentials offer a potentially inexpensive source of synthetic training data, but existing models often lack the accuracy needed to provide useful reference energies. Here, we introduce the density-based intermolecular potential (DensIP), a physics-based model of intermolecular interactions that uses machine-learned electron densities and only four universal parameters. We train and test DensIP on CCSD(T)/CBS interaction energies from DES15K, a dataset of dimers of small organic molecules. DensIP achieves sub-kcal/mol errors for dimers containing molecules absent from the training set, including molecules in non-equilibrium conformations, demonstrating strong transferability. We further show that DensIP can be applied to molecules as large as drug ligands. Notably, DensIP outperforms state-of-the-art general-purpose MLFFs for long-range interactions, making it a promising approach for generating accurate synthetic training data at scale.

AI.tldr: DensIP is a physics-based intermolecular potential using machine-learned electron densities with only four universal parameters, achieving sub-kcal/mol CCSD(T)/CBS accuracy on the DES15K dataset and outperforming general-purpose MLFFs for long-range interactions, making it suitable for generating synthetic training data.
AI.motivation: Machine-learned force fields require large training datasets, but generating high-quality ab initio reference data is computationally expensive. Classical empirical potentials offer cheap synthetic data but often lack accuracy. A physics-based, accurate and transferable model for intermolecular interactions is needed.
AI.method: DensIP is a density-based intermolecular potential that combines machine-learned electron densities with only four universal parameters. It is trained and evaluated on CCSD(T)/CBS interaction energies from the DES15K dimer dataset of small organic molecules.
AI.result: DensIP achieves sub-kcal/mol errors on dimers containing molecules absent from the training set, including non-equilibrium conformations. It shows strong transferability, scales to drug-sized ligands, and outperforms state-of-the-art general-purpose MLFFs for long-range interactions.
AI.conclusion: DensIP is a promising approach for generating accurate synthetic training data at scale due to its accuracy, transferability, and scalability, addressing the data bottleneck in MLFF development.

title: Shaping liquids into space structures - microgravity-assisted design and manufacturing of minimal surfaces
summary: This work advances a fundamentally new approach to space-based construction by using liquid self organization in microgravity as a generative design and fabrication principle. Building on the LiquiFab method, we demonstrate how minimal surface architectures - traditionally dependent on complex additive manufacturing - can instead emerge directly from the physics of fluid interfaces shaped by programmable boundary conditions. We present a simulation-to-fabrication workflow, that includes a boundary-driven minimal-surface solver integrated in Grasshopper/Rhino, and an experimental system that implements in a neutral buoyancy environment simulating microgravity. This enables the generation of customizable Schwarz-P-inspired with tunable geometry and thickness, illustrating a scalable pathway for material-efficient, on-orbit fabrication. To validate performance in true microgravity, a flight experiment on the International Space Station is scheduled for the first quarter of 2027 and we here detail the additional considerations required for this experiment.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a novel approach to space-based construction using liquid self-organization in microgravity, where minimal surface architectures emerge directly from fluid interface physics rather than additive manufacturing. It includes a simulation-to-fabrication workflow with a boundary-driven minimal-surface solver integrated into Grasshopper/Rhino, and an experimental neutral buoyancy system that simulates microgravity. Customizable Schwarz-P-inspired structures with tunable geometry and thickness are demonstrated, with a flight experiment on the ISS scheduled for Q1 2027.
AI.motivation: Traditional space-based construction relies on complex additive manufacturing, which is resource-intensive and difficult to implement on-orbit. This work seeks a fundamentally new approach leveraging liquid self-organization in microgravity as a generative design and fabrication principle, enabling material-efficient construction without complex fabrication machinery.
AI.method: The work builds on the LiquiFab method, using programmable boundary conditions to shape fluid interfaces that naturally form minimal surface architectures. A simulation-to-fabrication workflow is developed, including a boundary-driven minimal-surface solver integrated into Grasshopper/Rhino for design generation, and an experimental neutral buoyancy system that emulates microgravity conditions for physical validation. Schwarz-P-inspired structures with tunable geometry and thickness are generated.
AI.result: The workflow enables the generation of customizable Schwarz-P-inspired minimal surface structures with controllable geometry and thickness, demonstrating a scalable pathway for material-efficient, on-orbit fabrication. A flight experiment on the International Space Station is scheduled for Q1 2027, with additional experiment-specific considerations detailed in the paper.
AI.conclusion: Liquid self-organization offers a viable alternative to additive manufacturing for space-based construction, providing a scalable and material-efficient pathway. The validated simulation-to-fabrication workflow, combined with the planned ISS flight experiment, establishes a practical route toward on-orbit fabrication of minimal surface architectures.

title: Time-Resolved Thermal Susceptibility Mapping via Low-Temperature Scanning Laser Microscopy
summary: We present a multiharmonic lock-in detection approach that utilizes the inverse Fast Fourier Transform to reconstruct the time evolution of thermal susceptibility with high spatial resolution. The method is implemented on a custom-built, modular scanning laser microscope designed for operation in low working-distance optical cryostats and thoroughly calibrated for spatial accuracy. A demonstrative case study using a superconducting resonator highlights the capability of this technique to generate thermal images on time scales significantly shorter than the intrinsic scanning speed, thus enabling dynamic thermal characterization with high spatial fidelity. The proposed technique of low-temperature time-resolved scanning laser microscopy offers unique opportunities to explore superconducting devices, 2D materials, hybrid planar structures, and other low-dimensional systems.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a multiharmonic lock-in detection technique using inverse Fast Fourier Transform to reconstruct the time evolution of thermal susceptibility with high spatial resolution, implemented on a custom scanning laser microscope for low-temperature operation.
AI.motivation: To enable dynamic thermal characterization of low-dimensional systems (superconducting devices, 2D materials, hybrid planar structures) with high spatial fidelity on time scales significantly shorter than intrinsic scanning speeds.
AI.method: A multiharmonic lock-in detection approach based on inverse Fast Fourier Transform reconstructs time-resolved thermal susceptibility images. The system uses a custom-built modular scanning laser microscope designed for low working-distance optical cryostats and is calibrated for spatial accuracy. A superconducting resonator serves as a demonstrative case.
AI.result: The technique successfully generates thermal images on time scales significantly shorter than the intrinsic scanning speed, demonstrated via a superconducting resonator case study, achieving high spatial resolution dynamic thermal characterization.
AI.conclusion: Low-temperature time-resolved scanning laser microscopy with multiharmonic lock-in detection provides unique opportunities for exploring superconducting devices, 2D materials, hybrid planar structures, and other low-dimensional systems through dynamic thermal imaging.

title: Doping-driven Mott transition from steady-state density functional theory
summary: The doping-driven Mott transition in the Hubbard model is described within the frame- work of steady-state density functional theory, or i-DFT. In order to access the many-body spectral function in i-DFT, an approximation for the exchange-correlation (xc) bias at arbitrary density and current is required. By using Fermi-liquid theory, a connection between the xc bias of i-DFT and the quasiparticle weight of many-body theory is derived and the results are employed to guide the construction of the approximation. Numerical results obtained with this functional demonstrate that the doping-driven Mott transition can indeed be captured with i-DFT.

AI.tldr: This paper applies steady-state density functional theory (i-DFT) to describe the doping-driven Mott transition in the Hubbard model. By deriving a connection between the exchange-correlation bias and the quasiparticle weight via Fermi-liquid theory, the authors construct an approximation for the xc bias and demonstrate numerically that i-DFT can capture the Mott transition.
AI.motivation: The goal is to extend i-DFT to access the many-body spectral function of the Hubbard model, which requires an approximation for the exchange-correlation bias at arbitrary density and current. The motivation is to demonstrate that i-DFT can capture the doping-driven Mott transition.
AI.method: The paper derives a connection between the xc bias of i-DFT and the quasiparticle weight using Fermi-liquid theory. This relation guides the construction of an approximate xc bias functional, which is then used within the i-DFT framework to compute spectral properties.
AI.result: Numerical results obtained with the constructed functional show that the doping-driven Mott transition can indeed be captured within i-DFT.
AI.conclusion: i-DFT, supplemented with a Fermi-liquid-based approximation for the xc bias, is capable of describing the doping-driven Mott transition in the Hubbard model.

title: Planar Nanofluidic Memristors Enabled by Surface Charge Gradient
comment: Main text: 7 pages, 4 figures. Supplementary material: 17 pages, 13 figures
summary: Nanofluidic memristors, exploiting ion transport in nanochannels, hold promise for neuromorphic applications. A planar architecture is particularly desired for scalable integration with established micro- and nanofabrication technologies. Here, using the Poisson-Nernst-Planck framework, we theoretically propose planar nanofluidic memristors enabled by surface charge gradient, providing an alternative to the commonly used geometrically asymmetric architectures. The resulting memristive behavior is governed by a diffusion-mediated secondary enrichment effect. By systematically solving the PNP equations, we obtain the scaling of the characteristic memory time across the parameter space. We also reveal that the memory effect is related to the first-order moment of surface charge, for arbitrary charge profiles. These results provide a theoretical basis for rationally designing and optimizing planar nanofluidic memristors through spatially patterned surface charge.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically proposes planar nanofluidic memristors enabled by surface charge gradients (rather than geometric asymmetry), using the Poisson-Nernst-Planck framework. The memristive behavior arises from a diffusion-mediated secondary enrichment effect, with memory time scaling characterized across parameter space and shown to relate to the first-order moment of the surface charge profile.
AI.motivation: Nanofluidic memristors are promising for neuromorphic applications, but commonly rely on geometrically asymmetric architectures that hinder scalable planar integration with established micro-/nanofabrication technologies. A planar design based on surface charge patterning offers a more fabrication-compatible alternative.
AI.method: The authors use the Poisson-Nernst-Planck (PNP) framework to systematically solve ion transport in planar nanochannels with surface charge gradients. They derive scaling laws for characteristic memory time across parameter space and establish a general relationship between the memory effect and the first-order moment of the surface charge for arbitrary charge profiles.
AI.result: The planar nanofluidic memristor exhibits memristive behavior governed by a diffusion-mediated secondary enrichment effect. The characteristic memory time scaling is obtained across the parameter space, and the memory effect is proven to be related to the first-order moment of surface charge for arbitrary charge profiles.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a theoretical foundation for rationally designing and optimizing planar nanofluidic memristors via spatially patterned surface charge, enabling scalable integration for neuromorphic applications.

title: Interplay of nonrelativistic and relativistic spin splittings in altermagnets
summary: Despite their compensated magnetic moments, altermagnets (AMs) exhibit nonrelativistic spin splitting (NRSS) that offers routes to spintronic functionality without relying on relativistic spin-orbit coupling. However, how NRSS influences relativistic phenomena remains largely unexplored. Here we show that NRSS plays a crucial role in reshaping the Rashba effect in AMs with broken inversion symmetry. Using a tight-binding model, we demonstrate that Rashba spin splitting, whose magnitude is typically limited by the strength of spin-orbit coupling, is governed by NRSS energy scales. The resulting Rashba bands combined with NRSS generate anomalously large charge-to-spin conversion with a Néel-vector-tunable spin polarization. First-principles calculations for the noncentrosymmetric AM GdAlSi corroborate the emergence of these effects in a real system. Our results reveal the interplay between nonrelativistic and relativistic effects in AMs and identify them as fertile platforms for spin-orbitronic applications.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals that nonrelativistic spin splitting (NRSS) in altermagnets (AMs) crucially reshapes the Rashba effect even in the absence of inversion symmetry. Using tight-binding and first-principles calculations (on GdAlSi), the authors show that Rashba spin splitting magnitude becomes governed by NRSS energy scales rather than solely spin-orbit coupling strength, and that the resulting Rashba bands combined with NRSS produce anomalously large charge-to-spin conversion with Néel-vector-tunable spin polarization. This establishes AMs as fertile platforms for spin-orbitronic applications.
AI.motivation: While altermagnets are known for their nonrelativistic spin splitting (NRSS) enabling spintronic functionality without spin-orbit coupling, the influence of NRSS on relativistic phenomena—specifically the Rashba effect—remains largely unexplored, prompting this investigation.
AI.method: The authors use a tight-binding model to analyze Rashba spin splitting in inversion-symmetry-broken altermagnets, demonstrating that its magnitude is governed by NRSS energy scales. They further perform first-principles calculations for the noncentrosymmetric altermagnet GdAlSi to corroborate the predicted effects in a realistic material.
AI.result: Rashba spin splitting in AMs is no longer limited by spin-orbit coupling strength alone but is controlled by NRSS energy scales. Combining Rashba bands with NRSS yields anomalously large charge-to-spin conversion with Néel-vector-tunable spin polarization, as confirmed by first-principles calculations on GdAlSi.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal a previously unknown interplay between nonrelativistic and relativistic effects in altermagnets, identifying them as fertile platforms for spin-orbitronic applications.

title: Aging Phase Diagram and Exact Asymptotic Energies of Mixed Spherical Spin Glasses
summary: We determine the aging phase diagram of mixed spherical $(p+s)$-spin glasses quenched from random configurations to zero temperature. Solving the asymptotic dynamical equations of Cugliandolo and Kurchan, we find transitions between aging states with one, two, and continuously many effective temperatures, including phases in which discrete and continuous hierarchies coexist. We obtain analytic expressions for the energies reached asymptotically by the dynamics. In models combining pairwise and higher-order interactions, and sufficiently separated interaction orders ($s>3$), a fully continuous phase exists, where the gradient descent relaxation converges to the algorithmic energy lower bound. Instead, in mixed models with only high-order interactions ($p\ge3$) the energy relaxation remains strictly above it. Numerical integration of the dynamical equations is consistent with the predicted two-step and mixed discrete--continuous aging states.

AI.tldr: This paper determines the zero-temperature aging phase diagram of mixed spherical (p+s)-spin glasses quenched from random configurations. By solving Cugliandolo-Kurchan asymptotic dynamical equations, the authors find transitions between aging states with one, two, and continuously many effective temperatures, including phases with coexisting discrete and continuous hierarchies.
